quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on weighting counts by their number of threads and what the two totals in the worksheet mean.

questions.q: What did Lecture 2 assume that Lecture 3 relaxes?
options: That all yarns have the same price
That there is one thread of each yarn
questions.explain: Lecture 2 took one thread of each count (equal shares); Lecture 3 weights each count by its number of threads, as in a stripe or selvedge.

questions.q: In the formula Mean Ne = Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne), the denominator is proportional to:
options: Total weight of the threads per unit length
questions.explain: threads ÷ Ne is proportional to the weight of those threads per unit length, so the sum is the total weight; the numerator Σ threads is proportional to total length.

questions.q: The quantity threads ÷ Ne for one yarn is largest when:
options: The yarn is fine and few threads
The yarn is coarse and many threads
The yarn is fine and many threads
questions.explain: Many threads and a low (coarse) Ne both raise threads ÷ Ne; such a yarn carries the greatest share of the warp weight.

questions.q: A slot in the worksheet with 0 threads has no effect on the mean count, whatever count is typed in it.
questions.explain: With 0 threads both Σ threads and threads ÷ Ne are 0 for that slot, so it adds nothing to either total.

questions.q: Which real warp features make yarns of different counts appear in unequal numbers?
questions.explain: The lecture names a stripe, a selvedge or a cord as cases where, say, 56 threads of one count run beside a few threads of another.

questions.q: If a warp has 56 threads of Ne 30 and 4 threads of Ne 10, the coarse threads make up about what share of the threads?
questions.explain: 4 ÷ 60 = 6.7 % of the threads — but, as the lecture shows, they carry about 18 % of the weight.

questions.q: A Ne 10 thread weighs how many times as much per unit length as a Ne 30 thread?
questions.explain: Weight per length is proportional to 1/Ne: (1/10) ÷ (1/30) = 3, so each coarse thread weighs three times a fine one.

questions.q: When all the threads in the worksheet are the same count, the mean count equals that count regardless of the thread numbers.
questions.explain: Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = Σ threads ÷ Ne when Ne is common, so the ratio returns the same Ne — as in the default sheet where A and B are both Ne 30 and the mean is 30.00.

questions.q: The mean count found by this method is a:
questions.explain: Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne) is a thread-weighted harmonic mean of the counts, which is what an indirect count system requires.

questions.q: Adding a few coarse threads to a warp of fine threads always moves the mean count:
options: Up or down depending on price
questions.explain: Coarse threads add weight faster than length, so the mean count drops; the lecture example falls from Ne 30 to about Ne 26.5 with only 7 % coarse threads.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The weighted mean-count formula, its two totals and how the mean responds when threads or counts change.

questions.q: The mean count of yarns in proportion is:
questions.explain: Total length over total weight: Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne). The first option is a thread-weighted arithmetic mean, which overstates the count; the third is its reciprocal.

questions.q: In the default worksheet Σ threads = 60.35 and Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 2.0117. The mean count is therefore:
questions.explain: Mean Ne = 60.35 ÷ 2.0117 = 30.00, confirming both yarns are Ne 30.

questions.q: Doubling the number of threads of every yarn in the warp changes the mean count by:
questions.explain: Both totals double, so their ratio is unchanged; only the proportions between yarns matter, not the absolute numbers.

questions.q: If the coarse yarn in a stripe is replaced by an even coarser one (lower Ne), the mean count:
options: Becomes equal to the fine yarn
questions.explain: A lower Ne raises threads ÷ Ne for that yarn, enlarging the weight total, so the mean count falls further.

questions.q: The thread-weighted arithmetic mean Σ(threads × Ne) ÷ Σ threads gives the same result as the lecture formula.
questions.explain: For 56 × Ne 30 and 4 × Ne 10 the arithmetic mean is 28.67, but the true mean is 26.47; Ne is indirect so reciprocals must be weighted.

questions.q: The weight share of one yarn in the warp is:
questions.explain: threads ÷ Ne is proportional to weight, so the share of the weight total is that yarn's weight share; threads ÷ Σ threads is only its share of the thread count.

questions.q: With two yarns of counts N₁ and N₂ and thread numbers t₁ and t₂, the mean count written out is:
questions.explain: This is Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne) for two yarns; with t₁ = t₂ = 1 it reduces to Lecture 2's 2 ÷ (1/N₁ + 1/N₂).

questions.q: In the worksheet, 4.35 threads of Ne 30 give a threads ÷ Ne value of:
questions.explain: 4.35 ÷ 30 = 0.1450; 1.8667 is 56 ÷ 30 for yarn A and 130.5 would be threads × Ne.

questions.q: The mean count can never be lower than the coarsest yarn or higher than the finest yarn in the mix.
questions.explain: A weighted mean of this kind always lies between the extreme counts; the weighting only decides where between them it falls.

questions.q: Removing the coarse yarn B altogether (threads set to 0) from a warp of Ne 30 A threads returns the mean count to:
questions.explain: With only Ne 30 threads left the ratio of totals gives exactly Ne 30.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Mean counts of warps with unequal numbers of threads — give answers to two decimal places unless told otherwise.

questions.q: A warp has 56 threads of Ne 30 and 4 threads of Ne 10. What is the mean count?
In the same warp (56 × Ne 30, 4 × Ne 10), what percentage of the yarn weight is in the Ne 10 threads? One decimal place.
questions.explain: Weight share = 0.4 ÷ 2.2667 = 17.6 % — about 18 %, from only 7 % of the threads.

questions.q: What is the threads ÷ Ne value for 56 threads of Ne 30? Four decimal places.
questions.explain: 56 ÷ 30 = 1.8667, the first worksheet row.

questions.q: A warp has 100 threads of Ne 20 and 100 threads of Ne 40. Mean count?
questions.explain: Σ threads = 200; Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 5 + 2.5 = 7.5; mean = 200 ÷ 7.5 = Ne 26.67 — the same as Lecture 2's equal-share result.

questions.q: A sheeting warp has 3,000 ends of Ne 40 and a 200-end cord of Ne 20. Mean count?
questions.explain: Σ threads = 3,200; Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 75 + 10 = 85; mean = 3,200 ÷ 85 = Ne 37.65.

questions.q: Three yarns: 40 threads of Ne 20, 30 threads of Ne 30 and 30 threads of Ne 60. Mean count?
questions.explain: Σ threads = 100; Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 3.5; mean = 100 ÷ 3.5 = Ne 28.57.

questions.q: A warp uses 2,000 ends of Ne 30 and 500 ends of Ne 30 from a second lot. Mean count?
questions.explain: Both lots are Ne 30, so Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 2,500 ÷ 30 and the mean is exactly Ne 30.

questions.q: What is the threads ÷ Ne value for 60 threads of Ne 24? Two decimal places.
questions.explain: 60 ÷ 24 = 2.50, proportional to the weight of those 60 threads per unit length.

questions.q: A warp has 90 threads of Ne 45 and 10 threads of Ne 15. The mean count is:
questions.explain: Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 2 + 0.667 = 2.667; 100 ÷ 2.667 = Ne 37.5. Ne 42 is the thread-weighted arithmetic mean, the usual mistake.

questions.q: A stripe repeat has 20 threads of Ne 60 and 20 threads of Ne 20. The mean count is:
questions.explain: Equal threads: 40 ÷ (20/60 + 20/20) = 40 ÷ 1.333 = Ne 30. Ne 40 is the simple average.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Mill situations where threads of different counts share a warp and the mean count decides weight, yarn order and sizing.

questions.q: A stripe shirting has 95 % Ne 40 ends and 5 % Ne 10 ends. A colleague says the coarse ends are too few to matter for weight. What do you reply?
options: The Ne 10 ends weigh four times as much each, so they carry about 17 % of the warp weight and must be included
They matter only for the weft
They only matter if they are plied
questions.explain: Weight share = (5/10) ÷ (95/40 + 5/10) = 0.5 ÷ 2.875 = 17 %. Ignoring them understates yarn requirement and fabric weight.

questions.q: You are ordering warp yarn for a cord fabric with ends of two counts. Which figure do you need first to estimate total warp weight?
options: The simple average of the two counts
The thread-weighted mean count from Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ Ne)
questions.explain: Warp weight depends on total length divided by mean count; only the weighted harmonic mean gives the correct weight for mixed counts.

questions.q: A warp of 4,000 ends of Ne 40 gets a 100-end selvedge of Ne 20 on each side. What happens to the mean count?
questions.explain: 200 coarse ends add weight faster than length: 4,200 ÷ (100 + 10) = Ne 38.2, a little below 40.

questions.q: For sizing-paste calculations on a warp with mixed counts, using the simple average of the counts would under-estimate the warp weight.
questions.explain: The simple average is higher (finer) than the true mean count, so the warp would seem lighter than it is, and size take-up and chemicals would be under-planned.

questions.q: The worksheet has four slots but your warp has only two counts. What do you enter in slots C and D?
questions.explain: The lecture says to leave the threads of an unused slot at 0; it then contributes nothing to either total.

questions.q: A dobby stripe uses 56 ends of Ne 30 and 4 ends of Ne 10 per repeat. The designer wants the fabric lighter. Which change helps most?
options: Replace the Ne 10 ends with Ne 20
Replace 4 of the Ne 30 ends with Ne 40
Nothing — only the weft affects weight
questions.explain: The 4 coarse ends carry 18 % of the weight; halving their weight (Ne 10 → Ne 20) lifts the mean count from 26.5 to 29.0. Changing 4 fine ends to Ne 40 barely moves it.

questions.q: A trainee computes mean count by the formula but gets a value lower than the coarsest yarn. What has most likely happened?
options: The totals were inverted: Σ(threads ÷ Ne) ÷ Σ threads was taken
The threads were entered as a percentage
questions.explain: The mean must lie between the extreme counts; a result outside that range signals an arithmetic error such as dividing the wrong way or mis-entering a count.

questions.q: Two mills quote fabrics with 'average warp count Ne 30'. Mill A has all ends Ne 30; Mill B has a mix of Ne 40 and Ne 20 in equal numbers. Which statement is right?
options: Mill B's true mean is Ne 26.7, so its fabric is heavier than Mill A's
Both fabrics have the same warp weight
Mill B's true mean is Ne 30
questions.explain: Equal numbers of Ne 40 and Ne 20 give 2 ÷ (1/40 + 1/20) = Ne 26.7, not 30; Mill B's warp is heavier for the same ends per inch.

questions.q: A towel warp has 2,400 pile ends of Ne 16 and 1,200 ground ends of Ne 24. For yarn purchase you need the mean count. It is:
questions.explain: 3,600 ÷ (2,400/16 + 1,200/24) = 3,600 ÷ (150 + 50) = Ne 18. Ne 18.67 is the thread-weighted arithmetic mean.

questions.q: A buyer insists the fabric be described by a single warp count. Which count should the mill state for a warp of 56 × Ne 30 and 4 × Ne 10?
questions.explain: Ne 26.5 reproduces the true weight of the warp; stating Ne 30 would understate the weight by about 12 %.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Reverse problems, weight shares and comparisons that need two steps of reasoning about weighted counts.

questions.q: A warp has 56 threads of Ne 30. How many threads of Ne 10 must be added to bring the mean count down to exactly Ne 25? Two decimal places.
In a warp of 56 × Ne 30 and 4 × Ne 10, what percentage of the threads is Ne 10? One decimal place.
questions.explain: 4 ÷ 60 = 6.7 % of the threads, compared with 17.6 % of the weight.

questions.q: Which warp has the lower (coarser) mean count?
questions.explain: Means: first 100 ÷ (2.25 + 1) = 30.8; second 100 ÷ (1.25 + 2.5) = 26.7; third 30; fourth 100 ÷ (2.22 + 0.83) = 32.7. Half the ends at Ne 20 give the coarsest mean.

questions.q: A warp of 1,000 ends has a mean count of Ne 24 and contains 800 ends of Ne 30. What is the count of the other 200 ends? One decimal place.
questions.explain: Σ(threads ÷ Ne) = 1,000 ÷ 24 = 41.667; the Ne 30 ends give 26.667, leaving 15.0 for 200 ends, so Ne = 200 ÷ 15 = 13.3.

questions.q: If every thread in a warp were replaced by one of exactly half its Ne, the mean count would halve.
questions.explain: Halving every Ne doubles every threads ÷ Ne term, so Σ(threads ÷ Ne) doubles while Σ threads is unchanged, and the mean count halves: 56 × Ne 15 with 4 × Ne 5 gives Ne 13.24, half of 26.47.

questions.q: A student uses tex instead of Ne in the lecture formula Σ threads ÷ Σ(threads ÷ count). Why is the result wrong?
options: Tex is direct, so weights add as threads × tex and the mean tex is Σ(threads × tex) ÷ Σ threads
Tex cannot be averaged at all
Tex must first be converted to denier
The formula only works for cotton
questions.explain: In a direct system weight per length is the count itself, so the mean is a plain thread-weighted average of tex; the reciprocal form is only for indirect counts like Ne.

questions.q: A warp has 3,000 ends of Ne 40 and 200 ends of Ne 20 (mean Ne 37.65). If the 200 ends are changed to Ne 40, by how much does the mean count rise? Two decimal places.
questions.explain: All Ne 40 gives a mean of exactly 40; 40 − 37.65 = 2.35.

questions.q: Two warps each have 100 ends: W1 has 50 × Ne 20 and 50 × Ne 40; W2 has 50 × Ne 10 and 50 × Ne 80. Which has the coarser mean count?
questions.explain: W1: 100 ÷ (2.5 + 1.25) = 26.7; W2: 100 ÷ (5 + 0.625) = 17.8. The same simple average (30) hides very different weights.

questions.q: A warp of 56 × Ne 30 and 4 × Ne 10 is 100 m long. Using 1 Ne = 590.67 tex, what is the warp weight in grams? Nearest gram.
questions.explain: Ne 30 = 19.69 tex and Ne 10 = 59.07 tex (grams per 1,000 m). Per 100 m: 56 × 1.969 g + 4 × 5.907 g = 110.3 + 23.6 = 133.9 ≈ 134 g. The same comes from 6,000 thread-metres at the mean Ne 26.47 (22.32 tex).

questions.q: Why does the lecture call threads ÷ Ne 'proportional to the weight' rather than 'equal to the weight'?
options: Because the actual weight also depends on the length considered (one hank, one metre, the whole warp)
Because Ne is a direct system
Because threads are counted in pairs
Because weight is measured in tex
questions.explain: threads ÷ Ne gives pounds per thread-hank; multiplying by the actual length in hanks gives the real weight, so only the ratio between yarns matters for the mean.
